records.our_prose: Edamame is a soybean you eat as plump green pods, boiled or steamed in the pod and popped straight into your mouth. It grows like a bush bean: you plant the seeds in the garden after the last frost once the soil is warm, and the sturdy plants need no trellis. But edamame takes longer than green beans, about 75 to 100 days, and the big difference is that the whole plant ripens at once. Instead of picking for weeks, you harvest the whole plant in one go when the pods are plump and green, and the best window is only a few days. Soybeans flower by day length, so pick a variety suited to your area, and use a soybean inoculant on the seed, not the regular bean kind. Always cook edamame before eating it.

records.our_prose: Flat young pods form where the flowers were, then plump rapidly as the seeds swell to fill them. Edamame is picked at the R6 stage, when the bright green pods are plump and the beans inside nearly touch but are still tender and sweet, not yet hard or yellowing. This and flowering are the moisture-critical stages; drought here gives thin, poorly filled pods.

records.our_prose: Edamame is ready when the pods are plump and bright green and the beans nearly touch inside but are still tender, before they get hard or turn yellow. The whole plant ripens at the same time, so harvest it all at once: pull up the plant and strip off the pods. The best window is only about four to ten days, so check every day as the pods fill and cook or freeze them the same day.

records.our_prose: Harvest edamame at the R6 stage, when the pods are plump and bright green with the beans filling about 80 to 90 percent of the pod and nearly touching inside, still tender and sweet rather than hard or yellowing. Because the whole plant ripens together, harvest it all in one or two passes, pulling or cutting the plant and stripping the pods. The prime window is short, only about four to ten days, so check daily as the pods plump and cook or freeze the same day.

records.our_prose: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), the most important leaf-feeding beetle of soybeans. Overwintered adults move into seedlings in spring, and a later summer generation feeds on the pods, which is the costly stage. It also transmits bean pod mottle virus.

records.our_prose: Round to irregular holes chewed through the leaves, and on the pods the more damaging sign: chewing on the pod wall and, late in the season, clipping at the base of the pod that drops it entirely. The adult is a small reddish to yellowish beetle with a black triangle behind the head and usually a row of black spots along each wing cover.

records.source_context: (Photo: Lee Jenkins Slide Collection) Based on current research, pod damage by adult bean leaf beetles is a direct yield loss and considered the most economically impactful injury they can inflict. (Figure 4). T his damage can cause complete pod loss when adults feed at the base of the pod. This type of injury is referred to as “pod clipping.” Adult damage to the outer pod wall also leads to the formation of pod lesions.

records.our_prose: St. George summers routinely reach 100°F in June, July, and August (USU Extension, Elevations for Washington County), so the spring edamame crop is picked before the worst of the heat and flowers and young pods abort before they fill. USU's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah lists no St. George fall or summer-replant window for this crop, so the season ends here rather than resuming with a second planting.

Because the whole plant matures together, edamame does not give a long, forgiving pick like green beans: the prime window is only about four to ten days, when the pods are plump and green and the beans nearly touch but are still tender. Picked past that, the beans turn starchy and the color dulls.
